401.quote_or_event: “The simpleton, not being able to acquire any learning for himself, goes into the assembly of the learned, and reciting as his own a stanza which he has learned from some schoolboy, exposes thereby his own ignorance.”
401.explanation: The Jain didactic quatrains mock the person who walks into a gathering of scholars with no learning of his own. Whatever he says there only shows how little he knows.
401.tie_back: Valluvar's player throwing dice with no board drawn is the same unprepared speaker. With nothing mastered, his attempt in the learned assembly can only fail.
401.source: Naladiyar, ch. 32 'Experience in (conducting of) assemblies', stanza 4 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)
401._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org. Close fit: both describe an unlearned man exposing himself in an assembly of the learned. This is a Tamil Jain text, not canonical scripture.

402.quote_or_event: “He who is ignorant of the truth, egoistical, greedy, without self-discipline, and who talks loosely, is called ill-behaved and void of learning.”
402.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana's lecture on the very learned puts loose talk among the marks of the person without learning. It sits next to ignorance and egoism.
402.tie_back: The Kural mocks the unlearned man who longs to be heard as an orator. Jain teaching likewise treats eagerness to talk without learning as a sign of the empty, ill-disciplined person.
402.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 11.2 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
402._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. The verse links ignorance and loose talk but has no equivalent of the Kural's striking simile, so the fit is partial.

403.quote_or_event: “One should always be meek, and not be talkative in the presence of the wise; one should acquire valuable knowledge, and avoid what is worthless.”
403.explanation: Mahavira's first lecture on discipline tells the pupil to stay meek and quiet before the wise and to spend his effort gaining real knowledge.
403.tie_back: Valluvar says the unlearned can still be counted good if they keep silent before the learned. The Jain rule of discipline asks for exactly that silence in the presence of the wise.
403.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 1.8 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
403._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Near one-to-one on keeping quiet before the wise. The Jain verse is addressed to a monk-pupil rather than to the unlearned in general.

404.quote_or_event: “Clever talking will not work salvation; how should philosophical instruction do it? Fools, though sinking lower and lower through their sins, believe themselves to be wise men.”
404.explanation: The lecture on the false ascetic warns that clever words do not make a person wise. Fools mistake their own cleverness for wisdom.
404.tie_back: The Kural says the wise will not accept an unlearned man's cleverness, however fine it looks. The Jain verse likewise refuses to count mere cleverness as wisdom.
404.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 6.10 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
404._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Strong on rejecting cleverness without real knowledge. However, the Jain verse is about salvation, not about how the learned judge someone, so the fit is thematic.

405.quote_or_event: Indrabhuti Gautama, a renowned Vedic scholar with 500 disciples, went with bruised pride to debate Mahavira. Mahavira greeted him by name and answered his unspoken doubt about the existence of the soul. Indrabhuti's pride gave way, and he became Mahavira's first and chief disciple, Gautamaswami.
405.explanation: Jain tradition remembers the chief ganadhara's conversion as the moment a proud man's self-esteem melted in the presence of one who truly knew.
405.tie_back: Valluvar says an unlearned man's self-esteem withers once he talks with the learned. Indrabhuti's pride likewise dissolved the moment he spoke with Mahavira.
405.source: Jain narrative tradition of Indrabhuti Gautama's conversion, as retold in 'Gautamswami' (jainworld.com Jain stories)
405._accuracy_note: Paraphrased from a Jain educational retelling, not primary scripture. Indrabhuti was a great scholar, not an unlearned man, so the story matches only the 'pride melts before the truly learned' part of the kural.

406.quote_or_event: “Though great stones do not understand the speech of men, yet since they do what is required of them, as standing, sitting, lying down, or moving, they are far more useful than a fool (as it is impossible to induce a fool to act as we wish him).”
406.explanation: The Naladiyar's chapter on ignorance ranks the fool below even dead stones. Stones are at least of some use, while the fool yields nothing.
406.tie_back: Valluvar says the unlearned merely exist, like barren saline land that bears nothing. The Naladiyar similarly calls the fool more useless than lifeless stone.
406.source: Naladiyar, ch. 34 'Ignorance', stanza 4 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)
406._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org. Both use the image of a fruitless, lifeless thing for the unlearned, though the images differ (stone versus salt land). This is a Tamil Jain text.

407.quote_or_event: “In the seagirt earth merit is various. The sensible should be great. Those who are foolish, and are like unbeaten steel and the thorny brinjâl, will flourish in silk and gay apparel.”
407.explanation: The Naladiyar notes that fools may be dressed in silk and finery while staying as crude and useless as unworked steel or a thorny plant.
407.tie_back: The Kural compares the good looks of someone without understanding to a painted clay doll. The Naladiyar likewise sees only fine outer show over an unformed, empty inside.
407.source: Naladiyar, ch. 27 'Riches without goodness', stanza 4 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)
407._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org. Partial fit: both contrast outer adornment with inner emptiness, but the Naladiyar's point concerns undeserved prosperity rather than physical beauty. This is a Tamil Jain text.

408.quote_or_event: “If you ask what is the reason why, while the good and just are in poverty, the unjust and unlearned are wealthy, O thou who hast eyes elongated like a lance! when one investigates the matter, it is nothing else but the effect of deeds done in, a former birth.”
408.explanation: The Jain quatrain faces the same scandal as the Kural, the wealthy unlearned and the poor good, and explains it by karma carried over from earlier births. Its neighbouring stanza (27.7) adds that the wise would desire neither state.
408.tie_back: Valluvar judges wealth in the hands of the unlearned to be worse than the poverty of the good. The Naladiyar sets out the same pairing and puts it down to karma, not merit.
408.source: Naladiyar, ch. 27 'Riches without goodness', stanza 5 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)
408._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org, including the stray comma in the source. Same pairing as the kural, but the stanza explains it by karma instead of judging which state is worse. This is a Tamil Jain text.

409.quote_or_event: “Harikêsa-Bala was born in a family of Svapâkas (Kândâlas); he became a monk and a sage, possessed of the highest virtues, who had subdued his senses.” … “The value of penance has become visible, birth appears of no value! Look at the holy Harikêsa, the son of a Svapâka, whose power is so great.”
409.explanation: The Harikesa lecture tells of a monk born an outcaste who outshines the high-born Brahmin priests who mock him. In the end even they admit that birth counts for nothing beside spiritual attainment.
409.tie_back: Valluvar says the high-born unlearned are worth less than the learned of low birth. The Harikesa story makes the same point that inner worth outranks birth, with a low-born sage surpassing proud high-born priests.
409.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 12.1, 12.37 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
409._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Strong fit on worth over birth. The Jain text values penance and self-control rather than book-learning as such, so the parallel is close but not exact.

410.quote_or_event: “As a pig leaves a trough filled with grain to feed on faeces, so a brute (of a man) turns away from virtue, and takes to evil ways. Hearing a man thus compared to a dog and a pig, he who desires his own welfare, should adhere to good conduct.”
410.explanation: Mahavira's discipline lecture compares the person who turns from good teaching to animals that choose filth over grain.
410.tie_back: Valluvar says the unlearned compare with the learned as beasts compare with men. The Jain verse uses the same animal comparison for those who turn away from instruction.
410.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 1.5–6 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
410._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. The man-versus-beast comparison is shared, but the Jain verse is about turning from virtue and discipline rather than lacking learning as such.
